title: Sword Duel Pitch
eyebrow: AjsCanadaPrty · game pitch and prototype plan · nothing built yet

short.lead: Working title: Maple Blade. It is a first-person sword duel for the living room. Your phone, held upright like a hilt, becomes the sword on the TV. You swing to attack and hold a guard to block, and the first fighter to land three hits wins. It runs on RockSkipping's phone-controller stack. That stack already turns a phone's tilt into an exact 3D rotation in Unity, so the prototype can go straight to combat feel.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it produces and what it needs from you. P0 to P4 are the five prototype milestones, explained under Prototype milestones. The sections below are the pitch, and the choices at the end are yours.

changes: new
The fantasy: a Wii-style duel on a Canadian dock
Pick up your phone, and it is a sword.

You stand on a dock at Lake Louise facing a lumberjack, and both of you have swords. The camera is first person, so most of the screen is the two blades and the opponent behind them. He winds up and his blade glints. You raise your phone across his line, the blades clang, and sparks fly. Block at the last moment and he staggers, giving you a free swing. Three maple leaves fill up for each fighter, and the first to three wins. The pitch in one line: it is the Wii sword duel, played with the phone already in everyone's pocket, with nothing to install.
RockSkipping shows that phones can work as couch motion controllers with no app. It is a turn-based throwing game.
A real-time, one-on-one combat game on the same controller stack.
AjsCanadaPrty becomes a second game on technology you already own and have verified.

changes.alt: First-person concept frame of a sword clash on a dock with a PARRY call-out
changes.caption: The core moment: the blades cross, sparks fly, and the game calls PARRY. The HUD shows hits as maple leaves, and you are at one of three.

changes: new
The controls: the phone is the hilt
Hold it upright with the screen facing left or right, and your thumb on the screen.

The phone's top edge is the blade, so turning your wrist turns the sword one-to-one. The screen faces sideways, so from your eyes you see the phone's edge, the way you would see a sword's spine. Your thumb rests on a large grip pad on the screen. In the suggested design the sword is only live while your thumb is down, which works like the Wii's trigger and stops accidental swings while you talk or put the phone down. This pose was the hardest one for RockSkipping's old angle maths: an upright phone sits exactly at gimbal lock, the position where angle readings stop working. RockSkipping already fixed that by sending quaternions (four numbers that describe any rotation exactly) instead of angles, so this game inherits a pipeline that works in precisely this grip. Phones only report rotation, not position, so the sword's position comes from a simple shoulder-and-elbow arm model, as the early VR controllers did.
sensors.js turns phone tilt into an exact rotation, and PhoneAttitude.cs applies it in Unity. The neutral pose is the phone lying flat.
A sword neutral pose (upright) and an arm model that turns rotation into a believable sword position.
The motion code is reused rather than written again.

changes.alt: Diagram of the phone held upright as a sword hilt, from the side and from the player's eyes, with phone axes mapped to sword axes
changes.caption: The phone's top edge maps to the blade, its sideways axis to the cutting edge, and the screen direction to the flat of the blade.

changes: new
The move set for the prototype
Three swings, three guards, and a parry.

Attacks reuse RockSkipping's throw detector, which watches for a hard swing followed by a sudden stop. That stop is how a throw is released today. The phone's gyroscope reports which axis you rotated around, and that gives the swing's direction: overhead, left cut or right cut. Guards are read from the sword's pose when the attack lands: blade level overhead is a high guard, and blade upright on either side is a left or right guard. A guard that arrives in the last moment before impact is a parry. It staggers the opponent and opens a counter window. To beat the Wii's best-known exploit, where players flicked their wrists instead of swinging, a swing must sweep at least 60 degrees. That number is a starting value, to be tuned in P1.
throw.js detects one swing-and-stop per turn.
A swing reader that also reports direction, and a guard reader in Unity.
The input is easy to learn, and every swing produces a clear sound and spark.

changes.alt: Diagram of three swing arrows (overhead, left cut, right cut) and three guard bars (high, left, right), with parry explained
changes.caption: Each swing direction has a matching guard. Timing a guard late turns a block into a parry.

changes: new
The opponents: four Canadian NPC tiers
Training Post, Lumberjack Lou, Voyageur Marie and Old Man Winter.

Each tier changes the same small set of settings: how long the wind-up warning lasts, how often the NPC blocks you, how wide your parry window is, how many attacks it chains together, and whether it fakes an attack. Training Post is a straw dummy in a toque that only attacks overhead and never blocks. Lumberjack Lou attacks from two directions and blocks a quarter of your swings. Voyageur Marie uses all three directions and chains attacks in pairs. Old Man Winter, the boss, fakes attacks and chains three. The prototype ships with the first two. The other two follow, and come with their own arenas. All timings are proposed starting values that nobody has tested yet.
Nothing is reused here, because RockSkipping has no opponents.
A shared fighter interface that an NPC brain drives now, and a phone can drive later.
Difficulty becomes a settings table you can tune without new code.

changes.alt: Four low-poly fighters lined up on a dock: a straw training dummy, a plaid lumberjack, a voyageur in a red cap and sash, and an icy old man
changes.caption: The four tiers. The first two are in the prototype.

changes: new
Difficulty is timing
Shorter warnings, smaller parry windows, and longer combos.

Every NPC attack has the same beats: a wind-up warning, a block window, a short parry window just before impact, then a counter window if you parried. Difficulty only changes how long each beat is. That keeps the game readable, because a harder opponent is faster rather than following different rules. Wi-Fi delay is the risk here. RockSkipping only ever needed a cosmetic aim preview to arrive on time. A sword that must block in time is more demanding, so P0 measures the real delay first, and a fixed allowance is added to every window, hidden from the player.
Nothing from you.
A timing model per attack, with the network allowance applied on top.
The P0 delay measurement decides whether the parry windows can be as tight as shown.

changes.alt: Timeline bars comparing wind-up, parry, impact and counter windows for three NPC tiers
changes.caption: One attack, three difficulties. The bars shrink and the beats stay the same.

changes: new
Arenas: low-poly Canada
Lake Louise Dock first, then Algonquin Maple Clearing and Yellowknife Ice Road.

The style matches RockSkipping: flat-shaded low-poly shapes, fog fading into the sky, and the same Lake Louise colours (sky, teal water and sunlight are taken from LakeLouiseLook.json). The dock reuses RockSkipping's Lake Louise backdrop pipeline (SVG to Blender to Unity), so the first arena costs the least. The maple clearing is an autumn arena for Voyageur Marie, and the ice road under the northern lights belongs to Old Man Winter.
LakeLouiseEnvironment.cs and the Blender backdrop build exist in RockSkipping.
One dock arena for the prototype, and two more later.
Choose the first arena in the Choices section below.

changes: new
Game feel: sound and effects
Every contact is loud, bright and brief.

On a clash: a metal clang picked from several variants, sparks at the exact crossing point, a two-frame white flash, and a tiny camera shake. On a hit: the game freezes for about 80 milliseconds, the opponent recoils, maple leaves burst, and a leaf fills on the HUD. On a parry: a lower ring, a slow-motion beat, and a PARRY call-out. On a swing: a whoosh whose pitch rises with swing speed. On the phone: a short buzz on Android. iPhone browsers do not support vibration, so iPhone players get sound only. The ambience is loons, lapping water and wind. Sounds are generated by RockSkipping's procedural sound tool where it can make them, and anything it cannot make is sourced later.
SfxDirector, ProceduralClips and tools/audio/generate-sfx.js exist in RockSkipping.
Clash, hit, parry and whoosh sounds, plus spark and leaf effects.
Nothing from you.

changes.alt: Low-poly autumn maple clearing with red and orange trees and a voyageur opponent
changes.caption: Algonquin Maple Clearing, Voyageur Marie's arena.

changes: new
Built on RockSkipping's stack
Most of the hard plumbing is reused, and the new work is combat.

The hotspot, offline HTTPS, relay, QR join, rejoin and sensor normalisation all carry over. The phone page gets a swing controller adapted from the throw controller, plus a grip pad screen. The relay itself is unchanged, and the wire format gains two message types: POSE, a lossy stream of the sword's rotation at around 30 to 50 times a second, and SWING, the attack event that Unity treats as final. That mirrors RockSkipping's AIM and THROW messages. Unity decides every hit, and the phone never simulates combat. The key structural choice is an interface for a fighter's brain. The NPC brain drives a fighter today, your phone drives yours, and player-versus-player later is just two phone brains, with no rewrite.

RockSkipping holds the relay, controller page and Unity networking. RockSkipping's grant proposal kit (docs/grant/04-work-packages.md in Ajw2003/RockSkipping) already proposes extracting them as a plugin called HandOff.
A sword rig, swing and guard readers, a combat resolver, bout rules and fighter brains.
How the code is shared is a choice below.

changes.alt: Three-column diagram of phone, relay and Unity parts, coloured as reused, adapted or new
changes.caption: Green parts are reused, yellow parts are adapted, and red parts are new.

changes: new
Prototype milestones
Five steps from a sword on screen to a playtest.

P0, the sword follows the phone: tilting the phone 10 degrees tilts the sword 10 degrees, with the screen facing either way, and the delay is measured. P1, swings and guards: at least 18 of 20 swings in each direction are read correctly. P2, the first bout: a first-to-three bout against Training Post, with sound, sparks and the hit freeze. P3, difficulty: Lumberjack Lou plays from the settings table, and parry and counter-attack work. P4, the playtest: five people who have not seen it each finish a bout without coaching past the tutorial. Player-versus-player is outside this plan. It gets its own proposal once the slice is fun.
docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md holds these as a draft.

changes: new
Risks I would flag to you
Delay, flying phones, and tired arms.

Delay: if the hotspot adds too much, blocks feel late. P0 measures it before any combat work starts, and the timing allowance absorbs a fixed amount. Flying phones: the Wii needed wrist straps for a reason, so the tutorial asks for a firm grip or a lanyard. The game also never asks for a full-power swing, because the swing reader cares about direction and sweep, not force. Fatigue: three hits should keep a bout under about two minutes. That is an estimate and has not been timed. Tracking drift: RockSkipping's reference pose follows the phone while it rests, which would slowly move your guard during a bout. The sword locks that reference at en garde and re-centres between points.
RockSkipping's calibration re-centres the reference pose while the phone is still.
A reference locked for the bout, re-centred between points, and a grip warning in the tutorial.
These are the things P0 and P1 must prove.
choices: How should AjsCanadaPrty get RockSkipping's controller stack?
Copy relay/, controller/ and the Unity networking code, record the source commit, and keep RockSkipping untouched. This is the fastest route to a playable sword.
Do the HandOff plugin extraction from RockSkipping's grant proposal kit, then use it in both games. Cleanest, but probably weeks of work before any combat.
Pulls in the whole game, including scenes and physics it does not need.
Copying first gets combat feel tested soonest. Once two games use the same code, the later HandOff extraction can be based on how it is really used.
How many swing directions in the prototype?
Easy to read on the TV and easy to tell apart from gyroscope data.
A thrust is a forward push, which phones measure poorly without position.
The most Wii-like, but the hardest to make fair over Wi-Fi delay.
Three directions keep P1's 18-out-of-20 target reachable. A thrust can come later.
Guard zone from the sword's pose
Unity checks which zone your blade covers when the attack lands.
Looks great when it works, and feels unfair when delay moves your blade.
Simple, but loses the point of holding a sword.
Zones forgive small amounts of delay while still asking you to move the sword.
Only while the thumb holds the grip pad
Lift your thumb and the sword lowers, so there are no accidental swings.
Always live, with a re-centre button
Fewer rules, but more stray swings between points.
This mirrors RockSkipping's tap-to-arm guard against accidental throws.
Reuses RockSkipping's backdrop pipeline and colours.
Autumn colours, with a new backdrop to build.
Night and northern lights, the most striking, and the most new art.
The dock costs the least art time, so the prototype's time goes to combat feel.
